draft.title: The nervous system
card: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system (CNS). It receives messages, sorts them and sends out instructions.
A receptor is a cell or organ that detects a change, called a stimulus. Eyes, ears and skin all contain receptors.
Neurons (nerve cells) carry fast electrical messages. A message passes from a receptor to the CNS, and then to an effector.
An effector is a muscle or gland that carries out the response. A muscle may contract, and a gland may release a substance such as sweat.
draft.remember: Receptor detects, neurons carry, CNS processes, effector responds.

a.q: Which part of the nervous system detects a stimulus?
a.why: A receptor is the part that detects a change in the surroundings or the body. An effector is tempting, but it carries out the response after the CNS has sent its instructions.
a.clue: Which part notices the change first?

b.q: Leila smells toast burning in the kitchen and walks over to turn off the toaster. Which row correctly names the receptor and the effector?
b.why: The nose detects the smell, so it is the receptor. The leg muscles carry out the response, so they are effectors. The brain is part of the CNS, which processes the message, so it is neither a receptor nor an effector.
b.clue: Which part detects the smell, and which part does the moving?

wants.brief: A simple flow diagram of the path of a message: stimulus, receptor, neurons carrying the message to the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), neurons carrying instructions to an effector (muscle or gland), response. Each stage is labelled with the words used in the card.
wants.why: It shows the order of the parts so students can see how a message travels.
